\chapter{Synthesis --- Two at a Time}
\label{ch:synthesis-double-object}
\hlchaptermodality{102}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can carry a four-turn exchange in which almost no noun appears.}

Complete ES-C47-sintesis-dos-a-la-vez: produce se la hago and say how many words in it name anything.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — two at a time}

\label{lesson:ES-C47-sintesis-dos-a-la-vez}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}I tell it to him,\textquotedblright{} in three words. (\emph{Se lo digo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Tienes el libro?} — \emph{Sí. ¿\textbf{Te lo} digo?} — \emph{Sí, y \textbf{se lo} dices a Ana.} — \emph{Y la comida — \textbf{se la} hago hoy.}
\end{quote}

Look at the last three lines. After the first sentence names the book, \textbf{not one noun does any work.} \emph{Te lo}, \emph{se lo}, \emph{se la} — six words that name nothing, and the conversation is perfectly clear to both speakers.

That is what all of this has been for. Fifteen chapters of object pronouns exist so that a conversation can stop repeating itself, and this is the point where the machinery is complete enough to see it happen.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two words carrying a whole sentence}]
\emph{Se la hago} is three words and it means \textquotedblleft{}I make \textbf{the meal} for \textbf{her}, today.\textquotedblright{} Two of the three are pronouns; between them they carry a person and a thing, neither of which is named anywhere in the sentence.

English cannot compress like this. \emph{I'll make it for her} needs five words and still spells out \emph{for}. Spanish puts both jobs in front of the verb, in a fixed order, and gets on with it.

The cost is the one you already know, doubled. Two pronouns are two promises that both things are still in the room. When you lose track of one of them, the sentence does not become wrong — it becomes about somebody else, and nobody will notice until it matters.

So the practice that pays here is not conjugation. It is keeping a conversation's furniture in mind while you talk.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four-turn exchange straight through
  \item \textquotedblleft{}te lo digo, se lo dices, se la hago\textquotedblright{} until the pairs feel like single words
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I make it for her\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Se la hago}}.) How many nouns are in that sentence? (\textbf{None}.) And what does each pronoun promise? (That its thing is \textbf{still in the room}.) Next: the past tense.
\end{tcolorbox}
